background.definition: Subclavian steal is the retrograde (reversed) flow of blood from the vertebral artery back into the ipsilateral subclavian artery. It may cause symptoms of vertebral insufficiency. The coronary-subclavian steal syndrome is the retrograde flow of blood from a grafted internal mammary artery back into the subclavian, resulting in myocardial ischemia. Both "steal syndromes" may coexist in the same patient.

list.listitem: Incidence of vertebral-subclavian steal in the general population is unknown.
Following coronary artery bypass graft (CABG), the incidence of coronary-subclavian steal ranges from 0.5% to 2% but may be underreported.
The prevalence of SAS is estimated to be 1.9% of the general population rising to 2.7% after 70 years.
In a study of 724 consecutive patients with planned CABG using the internal mammary artery, 8.1% were found to have angiographically significant SAS.
Persons with SAS are likely to have other manifestations of vascular disease including peripheral arterial disease, coronary artery disease, and carotid occlusive disease.
Atherosclerotic SAS (most common).
Thoracic outlet syndrome.
Less than 5% of cases of SAS are due to congenital anomalies, surgical repair of tetralogy of Fallot or coarctation of the aorta, prior local radiation, or Takayasu's vasculitis.
SAS results in lower distal arterial pressure permitting reversal of normal blood flow.

The vertebral artery is an important collateral for arm circulation when there is significant SAS. In the presence of significant SAS, blood flows from the ipsilateral vertebral artery back into the subclavian artery. The subclavian artery supplies blood to the arm via the axillary artery. In the presence of normal cerebral collateral circulation via the Circle of Willis, this diversion of blood will be asymptomatic.

Proximal SAS with a patent left internal mammary artery (LIMA) may cause the reversal of blood flow from a LIMA graft back into the subclavian artery precipitating anginal symptoms or (rarely) acute myocardial infarction.
The left subclavian artery is affected more frequently than the right.

Suspect subclavian steal when symptoms (arm claudication, dizziness, vertigo, syncope, and visual disturbances) are associated with arm exercise or head movement in persons with SBP difference more than 15 mm Hg between arms. B
Color Doppler ultrasound is the best initial test for diagnosis of subclavian steal. C

list.listitem: A difference in systolic blood pressure 15 mm Hg or more with a decreased radial pulse is typical. Patients may also have an ipsilateral bruit over affected subclavian artery plus.

Symptoms of vertebrobasilar insufficiency (syncope, dizziness, ataxia, vertigo, diplopia, nystagmus, and ipsilateral visual blurring) may occur, especially if symptoms occur during arm exercise or with head turning. Chronic upper limb ischemia was present in 11.4% in a series of 131 patients with vertebral-subclavian steal.
May cause angina pectoris or acute myocardial infarction following CABG using the LIMA. Incidence is estimated at 0.5% to 2%, but may be underreported.
Rarely patients may present with a combination of anginal symptoms and those of vertebrobasilar insufficiency.

Systolic blood pressure difference of 15 mm Hg or more is highly specific (90%) but not very sensitive (~50%) for the diagnosis of SAS. A difference in systolic blood pressure of more than 15 mm Hg could be a helpful indicator of vascular disease.

Color Doppler ultrasound has a 94% accuracy rate in diagnosing subclavian steal when compared to MRA (sensitivity is 88%, specificity is 94%, positive predictive value is 78%, and negative predictive value is 97%). Due to its low cost, non-invasiveness, and lack of contrast it is the preferred initial test.
Catheter digital subtraction angiography is the gold standard for evaluating the great vessels prior to surgical intervention.
Contrast-enhanced MRA with flow encoded MRI is a reliable diagnostic alternative.
Angiographic steal may not be clinically significant.
Suspect SAS if there is a systolic BP difference 15 mm Hg or more between arms and a decreased radial pulse with or without bruit over affected subclavian artery.
Subclavian steal may cause symptoms of vertebral insufficiency: dizziness, syncope, presyncope and (rarely) arm ischemia with arm exercise.
Color Doppler ultrasound is the best initial diagnostic test.
Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with subclavian artery stenting is the current treatment of SAS resulting in vertebral coronary artery steal. B

Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with subclavian artery stenting is the current treatment of SAS resulting in vertebral coronary artery steal. Bare metal stent is usually used. There is insufficient evidence to determine whether stenting has an added benefit over angioplasty alone in this setting.
Primary indication for intervention is severe symptoms (arm ischemia or claudication, syncope, dizziness, and vertigo).
The incidence of restenosis has been reported at 6% to 21%.
Treatment may also be considered for left subclavian stenosis more than 50% with planned LIMA grafting to the left anterior descending coronary artery.
It may also be recommended before dialysis shunt placement.
There are no RCTs that address the optimal management of SAS prior to CABG for prevention of subclavian-coronary artery steal.
The presence of subclavian stenosis (with or without steal) predicts total and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality independent of both CVD risk factors and existent CVD at baseline. B

After median 42 month follow up, patients treated with percutaneous transluminal angioplasty had 60% risk reduction for hemodynamic subclavian stenosis compared to conservative treatment (P < .0001). However, the risk of having a symptomatic stenosis at the time of follow up did not differ between the treatment groups (P = .3). B
